newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: FEATURE-SAUDI DATES REMAIN DELICACY AFTER 5,000 YEARS.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-SAUDI DATES REMAIN DELICACY AFTER 5,000 YEARS.

text.p: When Mary cried out in pain at the birth of baby Jesus, God told her to eat fresh dates to ease her anguish, says Islam's holy book, the Koran.

And 14 centuries ago, when Prophet Mohammad fasted all day during the holy month of Ramadan, Moslems believe he broke the fast at sunset by eating dates. It is a tradition continued until today by many of the world's one billion Moslems.
Dates -- known as tamer, balah and a string of other names in Arabic -- played a key role in Saudi life long before oil was discovered in the 1930s and brought wealth to the kingdom.

For more than 5,000 years the so-called "fruit of life" has been a staple food in the Middle East, first cultivated on desert oases and now produced on huge irrigated plantations across the region. ONE OF WORLD'S BIGGEST DATE PRODUCERS
Saudi Arabia, home to Islam's two holiest sites and the birthplace of Prophet Mohammad, is one of the world's biggest producers and consumers of dates.

The chewy, dark fruit is a popular treat in the kingdom and one of its main crops, with production hovering around 570,000 tonnes worth about $203 million in 1996 according to official figures and estimates. Connoisseurs say the dates grown in the kingdom are among the most delicious in the world.
Saudi date palms are considered so precious that all trees are tagged to ensure they are not illegally exported.
"We sell dates to the royal family," said Willem Walbers, the Belgian factory manager of the Bateel date company in Riyadh.
"For example, several times a year one member of the royal family buys dates worth 40,000 to 50,000 riyals ($11,000 to $13,000) each time," he said.
More than 100 kinds dates are produced in Saudi Arabia, with different areas famous for different specialities.
"In the holy city of Medina, for example, they produce a unique date which is smaller but mentioned by religious texts in association with Prophet Mohammad," Walbers said.
"It is the most expensive date at 300 to 400 riyals a kilo, and is so valuable that it is kept in a safe, even at the market," he said.

Another popular date -- called "Sukkary" which means "sugary" -- can be so hard you can shake it and hear the pit rattle. "You have to crack them open with a hammer and suck on them like a piece of sugar," Walbers said.
PRICES VARY
Date prices vary depending on the species, cleanliness and ripeness of the fruit. Retail prices range from one riyal to 80 riyals per kg (2.2 lb).

At Rabwa market in the Saudi capital Riyadh, rows and rows of long tables are laden with piles of the cheaper dates. Vendors shoo hordes of flies away from their sticky counters, beckoning customers to try their wares, from fresh dates in metal buckets to dates pressed in syrupy slabs.
"At markets, an average kilo of dates is over 50 percent infested with small worms and insect larvae," one expert said.

At high-tech date factories such as Bateel, dates are cleaner and prices are higher. And in addition to the traditional products such as fresh and pressed dates, Bateel caters to the upper end of the market with date biscuits, jam, sparkling juice and pralines made with Belgian chocolate.
ANCIENT CULTIVATION TECHNIQUES
Despite technological advances, date cultivation still relies on many of the techniques used thousands of years ago.
Pollination is encouraged by placing several male blossoms among the females, an ancient technique that requires a lot of climbing, experts say.

Barefoot men can still be seen scaling the rough trunks of the date palms -- which grow to heights of 20 to 30 metres (65 to 100 feet) -- to pollinate the trees, clear away some dates to give others more space and finally to pick the fruit.
Dates, some with sugar content of 98 percent, have about 50 calories a piece, but are rich in vitamins and minerals including potassium, iron, calcium and vitamins A and B.
Many Arabs believe dates also have medicinal value and say they help cure insomnia and ensure healthy pregnancies.
And dates are a little-known ingredient in Western products including British brown sauces, food industry sources say.
"Dates are also in the secret recipe for Coke," suggested one.
($1=3.75 riyals)
